'''Gerhard Wilhelm Goetze''' (June 19, 1930 – January 17, 2007) was a German-born Ph.D. researcher and inventor in [[atomic physics]]. He was primarily known for his work on the Moon-to-Earth [[Apollo TV camera]]  making live broadcast in both brilliant sunlight and pitch darkness possible.<ref name="Inventor Gratified">''[[Star-Gazette]]'', July 21, 1969 – "Westinghouse Inventor 'Gratified' with Moon Show".</ref> Goetze discovered the secondary electron conduction (SEC) effect which amplified light through high-speed electrons deposited in thin film storage targets.<ref name="Tube with highly porous target" /><ref>{{Cite journal|author1=Goetze, G. W. |author2=Boerio, A. H. |date=September 1964|title=Secondary electron conduction (SEC) for signal amplification and storage in camera tubes|journal=[[Proceedings of the IEEE]]|volume=52 |issue=9|issn=0018-9219|pages=1007–1012|doi=10.1109/PROC.1964.3230}}</ref> The SEC tube was additionally used in ground-based astronomy, inspection of [[integrated circuit]]s, electron-microscope-based biological tissue study, security, and night vision.<ref name="Night Fighters Enlist">''Stevens Point Journal'', September 16, 1966 – Night Fighters Enlist Latest from Science</ref><ref>''Star-Gazette'', July 21, 1969 – Westinghouse Inventor "Gratified" with Moon Show</ref> Goetze received ten patents for his inventions.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://patft.uspto.gov/netacgi/nph-Parser?Sect1=PTO2&Sect2=HITOFF&u=%2Fnetahtml%2FPTO%2Fsearch-adv.htm&r=0&p=1&f=S&l=50&Query=in%2Fgoetze-gerhard-w&d=PALL|title=Patent Database|last=Goetze|first=Gerhard W|website=United States Patent and Trademark Office}}</ref>

The images of the first man on the Moon are recorded through the work of Goetze.<ref name="Ray of Hope for Helping">''Star-Gazette'', August 24, 1969 – TV Used on Moon Seen as a Ray of Hope for Helping Blind</ref>

In 1973 Goetze received a [[Franklin Institute#Awards|Franklin Institute]] Award, the Longstreth Medal established in 1890, for the conception and development of the SEC tube, which played an important role in television, night surveillance and ultraviolet astronomical observations.<ref name="FranklinInstitute">[https://www.fi.edu/laureates/gerhard-w-goetze Gerhard W. Goetze] at the [[Franklin Institute]]; retrieved December 8, 2017</ref>

In 1984 Goetze was awarded the [[Rudolf-Diesel-Medaille]], an award by the German Institute for Inventions, for the applications of the secondary electron conduction tube in industry.<ref name="Diesel">* [https://dieselmedaille.de/?s=Gerhard+W+Goetze&submit=Suche Suchergebnisse zu: Gerhard W Goetze], at the [[:de:Deutsches Institut für Erfindungswesen|Deutsches Institut für Erfindungswesen]]; retrieved December 8, 2017</ref><ref name="Herbert Fritsche">{{Cite book|title=Eschwege Lexicon|last=Fritsche|first=Herbert|publisher=Thiele & Schwarz|year=2015|isbn=978-3-00-049311-9|location=Kassel, Germany|pages=242–243}}</ref>

== Biography ==

=== Early life and education ===
Gerhard W. Goetze was born in Niederdünzebach near [[Eschwege]], [[Hessen]], [[Germany]] on June 19, 1930, to Walter Kurt Götze, a businessman, and Anna Katherine Sieland. He attended the local primary school until his father was transferred to Bartenstein, near Königsberg, East Prussia, Germany to work at the local ''Volksschule'' (primary school).

Goetze attended the Volksschule from 1936 to 1944.<ref name="Herbert Fritsche" />

Goetze, along with his mother and baby sister, fled Bartenstein, now named [[Bartoszyce]], on the last train on January 22, 1945, during the [[evacuation of East Prussia]]. They made their way back to the family home in Niederdünzebach. Gerhard attended the ''Gymnasium'' or college preparatory school, the Friedrich-Wilhelm Schule in Eschwege from 1946 to 1949 where he received his ''[[Abitur]]'' diploma.<ref name="Herbert Fritsche" />

From 1949 to 1958 Goetze studied and taught physics at the [[University of Marburg]].<ref>Eschwege Lexicon, Herbert Fritsche, Theile & Schwarz, Kassel, 2015, pp 242-243.</ref> In 1951, he became a member of one of the oldest academic fraternities, the [[German Student Corps]], Saxonia,<ref>70 Jahre Turnerschaft in CC SAXONIA zu Marburg, 1886-1956, p. 126</ref> founded in 1886, with the motto ''In Treue Fest'' or "In Loyalty Firm".

His concentration in [[nuclear physics]] led to his doctoral thesis in ''Zerfallsschema und Beta-Spektrum des MsTh1 (Ra228)'' (Disintegration Schematic and Beta Spectrum of Mesothorium) ([[isotopes of radium]]).<ref>{{cite journal|title=Zerfallsschema und β-Spektrum des MsTh1 (Ra228)|first=Gerhard|last=Goetze|date=June 1, 1960|journal=Zeitschrift für Physik|volume=158|issue=3|pages=347–358|doi=10.1007/BF01340565|bibcode=1960ZPhy..158..347G |s2cid=121931054}}</ref> Goetze later found [[electron]]s to be more interesting and continued his work in atomic physics.<ref name="Ray of Hope for Helping"/>

=== Marriage and children ===
In 1954, Gerhard married Lisa Herta Kohlus of Eschwege. They had five children, two born in the convent of [[Vincent de Paul]] in Eschwege, Germany; Regina Karin and Martin Gerhard and three children born in Wilkinsburg, Pennsylvania, US; Frank Walter, Arleen Susan and Thomas Wilhelm. Their marriage ended in divorce.

He had a daughter with his second wife.<ref name="Herbert Fritsche" />

=== Emigration to the US ===
Goetze traveled from Germany to New York in January 1959 with his pregnant wife and two children under the sponsorship of the [[United States Department of the Army]] in the national interest. They lived for several months in the Alamac Hotel on Broadway and West 71st Street in New York City until employment was found.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Goetze, Gerhard Wilhelm|last=Goetze|first=Gerhard|date=January 1959|work=Joint Intelligence Objectives Agency, Room 2E961-G, The Pentagon}}</ref>

In the summer of 1959 the family moved to [[Monroeville, Pennsylvania]], where Goetze worked for the [[Westinghouse Electric Corporation]] Research and Development Laboratories in [[Pittsburgh]].<ref name="auto">Pittsburgh Post-Gazette, August 1, 1961 – New System Makes X-ray Brighter, New Electronic System Increases Light 1,000 Times.</ref><ref name="John Reisner">Pittsburgh Post-Gazette, November 1, 1963 – TV Camera Will See in Near-Darkness, Tube Developed by Westinghouse Will Send Back Pictures from Space</ref> His early research on [[night vision]] was initially classified for the Department of Defense.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Goetze|first=G.W.|date=September 1963|title=Applied research on SEC Amplification Camera Tube|journal=Defense Documentation Center for Scientific and Technical Information|volume=419120|pages=iii–28|via=Defense Documentation Center, Cameron Station, Alexandria, Virginia}}</ref> It was later declassified by the federal government after use along the South Vietnam frontier and for use by NASA and police anti-crime measures.<ref>{{Cite news|title='Owl Eye' at Night: City Police Propose Anti-Crime Measure|last=Mack|first=Dave|date=March 29, 1971|work=Press and Sun Bulletin}}</ref>

In 1964, he moved with his wife and five children to [[Elmira, New York]], to continue his work at the Westinghouse [[Cathode ray|Cathode Ray]] Tube facility in nearby Horseheads, New York. As operations manager, Goetze grew the department from a team of six to more than 170 scientists and staff.<ref name="Ray of Hope for Helping"/> His work through Westinghouse was an integral part of the NASA space program.

Goetze became a US citizen on July 4, 1967, in [[Ithaca, New York]]. At that time, he changed his name from Götze to Goetze.<ref>''Star-Gazette'', July 4, 1967 – Thirteen Area Persons were Naturalized in Ceremonies at the Tompkins County Supreme Court</ref>

=== Employment at Westinghouse ===
*1959-1964 – Scientific researcher and senior physicist, Westinghouse Research and Development Laboratories in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania.<ref name="auto"/><ref name="John Reisner"/>
*1964-1969 – Operations manager of the Image Tube Department at Westinghouse, Horseheads, New York.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Dr. Goetze Given Special Patent Award|date=August 28, 1969|work=Star-Gazette}}</ref>
*1969 – Academic sabbatical to attend the Sloan Business School, MIT, Massachusetts, US.
*1969-1983 – Various positions with Westinghouse International, Frankfurt, Germany with his last position as director of electronic components in Europe.<ref name="Westinghouse forms 2">{{Cite news|title=Westinghouse Forms 2 Foreign Marketing Units|date=October 28, 1970|work=Star-Gazette}}</ref>

=== Other positions ===
*1965-1969 – Named to the Defense Advisory Group on Electronic Devices, Office of the Secretary of Defense.<ref>''Star-Gazette'', July 24, 1966 – Dr. Goetze Named to Advisory Board</ref>
*1966 – Senior member of the [[Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers]].
*1970 – Civilian consultant to the Department of Defense as a member of the Advisory Group on Electronic Devices.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Gerhard W Goetze|date=September 6, 1970|work=Star-Gazette}}</ref>
*1970 – Adjunct professor for electrical engineering at [[University of Rhode Island]].<ref name="Westinghouse forms 2" />
*1973 – [[Franklin Institute]] – elected as a life fellow.

=== Business development in Germany ===
In 1981 Goetze headed Fanal Elektric, an electronic components manufacturer in Germany, who sold 95% of its stock shares to Westinghouse to secure the American Market. In 1989, Goetze along with other investors, purchased Fanal Elektric from Westinghouse and grew Fanal with 3 other firms; Hundt & Weber, Maihak Aktiengesellschaft and Fanalmatic GmbH into an international company under Goetze and Scheffler Group, GmbH.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Management Buy Out/Manager Kaufen Deutsche Töchter|date=May 10, 1989|work=Handelsblatt}}</ref> His firms employed over 1,000 people. The Goetze and Scheffler Group suffered a severe decline in sales with the financial catastrophe of [[Westinghouse Electric Corporation]] in the 1990s. The G&S Group ultimately closed as a business.

=== Personal life and soaring ===
Goetze's passion in life was for [[gliding]]. He began his interest at the Blaue Kuppe in the countryside of the [[Werra-Meißner-Kreis|Werra-Meißner area]]. Goetze was one of the early members (1964) of the Eschwege Luftsportverrein (local glider soaring club).<ref>{{Cite book|title=Chronik eines Traums, Von Fliegen an Werra und Meissner|last=Eschweger Luftsportverein|publisher=Koesel GmbH & Co. KG|year=2000|location=Kempten, Germany|pages=142}}</ref>

While living in Elmira, New York, Goetze spent many weekends with his family at the Harris Hill Soaring<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://harrishillsoaring.org/|title=Harris Hill Soaring Corporation – The soaring capital of America|website=Harrishillsoaring.org|language=en|access-date=January 4, 2018}}</ref> Club pursuing his hobby as a sailplane pilot.<ref>''Star-Gazette'', August 26, 1969 – Apollo TV Tube Inventor a Soaring Buff</ref> In 1969 Goetze traveled to [[Pikes Peak]] near Colorado Springs, Colorado for the final qualifying test for the prestigious 3 Diamond Badge in gliding from the [[FAI Gliding Commission]]. His airplane towed him to 2,000 feet above ground level and from there using only airwave [[Lift (soaring)|lift]], soared to an altitude of {{convert|28,000|ft|m|abbr=off|sp=us}}.)<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.ssa.org/BadgesAndRecords?show=blog&id=3105|title=Soaring Society of America|website=Ssa.org|access-date=January 5, 2018}}</ref>
[[File:Gerhard W Goetze and Schweizer sailplane.jpg|thumb|Goetze in a Schweizer sailplane]]
Goetze was a long-time member of the [[Soaring Society of America]] (SSA).<ref>The Soaring Society of America, Inc. 1978 Membership Roster, pg 233</ref>

Goetze was also a commercial pilot.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Commercial Pilot License, Certificate # 1541487|last=Goetze|first=Gerhard|date=1972}}</ref>

He continued his joy for flying his entire life. His last aircraft, a 1960 single engine [[Cessna 182 Skylane]] was flown in 2007 after his death by his two sons, Frank, senior pilot for FedEx and Thomas, mechanical engineer, across the Atlantic Ocean over 10 days and 40 flight hours from [[Kassel Airport]], Germany to [[Beaver County Airport]], Pennsylvania via Denmark, Norway, the [[Faroe Islands]], Iceland, Greenland and Canada.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Goetze|first=Frank|date=Summer 2007|title=Flight from Germany to USA|journal=FAA Pilot Logbook}}</ref>

=== Death ===
Goetze died on January 17, 2007, in [[Bad Zwesten]], Germany at the age of 76 after suffering a severe stroke a month earlier.<ref name="Herbert Fritsche" />

He is buried in the local cemetery in his home village in Niederdünzebach (Eschwege), Germany.

== Scientific career, Westinghouse and Department of Defense ==
In October 1960 at the Fifth International Congress on High Speed Photography, A. Anderson, manager of the applied physics department of Westinghouse Research Laboratories stated that, "a new electronic tube, so sensitive it can 'see' individual particles of light, has enabled Westinghouse scientists to photograph the faint tracks of [[cosmic ray]] as they move through solid crystal at speeds near the velocity of light." The Astracon, light amplifier tube, was brought to practical application by Goetze. His research was supported in part by the [[United States Atomic Energy Commission]] and the [[United States Army Corps of Engineers]].<ref>{{Cite news|title=Westinghouse Image Tube, the Astracon, Used to Photograph Cosmic Ray Tracks|date=October 1960|work=Westinghouse News}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|title=Looking "Inside" Matter|date=November 1961|work=Westinghouse R&D Letter}}</ref>

In the early 1960s in the Pittsburgh research laboratories the SEC (secondary electron conduction) effect was discovered by Goetze.<ref name="John Reisner"/><ref>{{Cite book|last=Reisner|first=John|date=June 27, 1973|title=Committee on Science and the Arts Case No. 3526|publisher=Franklin Institute}}</ref> This was developed for the Department of Defense (DoD) for [[Night vision]] in Vietnam. It had the capability to produce clear images in motion at low light levels without motion distortion.<ref name="Night Fighters Enlist" />

The SEC tube had DoD highly top secret security classification<ref name="Steven-Boniecki">{{Cite book|title=Live TV From the Moon|last=Steven-Boniecki|first=Dwight|publisher=Apogee Books|year=2010|isbn=9781-926592-16-9|location=Burlington, Ontario, Canada|pages=113–159}}</ref> but was the only device that could meet the Apollo camera mission requirements to operate in both lunar day and night. The DoD was asked to allow Westinghouse the use of the SEC tube for the Apollo TV Camera program. The task to develop this unique SEC tube was headed by Goetze at the Westinghouse Tube Division in Elmira, New York.<ref name="Steven-Boniecki" />

The SEC tube was used to build a camera to transmit live images from the Moon to Earth on [[Apollo 11]]. The tube was also employed in science in [[electron microscope]] biological tissue study; ground-based astronomy, material testing and inspection of integral circuits in industry, and security and police.<ref name="Ray of Hope for Helping"/>

The SEC tube was used on the [[Orbiting Astronomical Observatory]] as the main sensor, on Apollo 9, 10, 11, 12, and 13, in the ATM Satellites as well as the OSO-H and SAS-D space projects.

The [[Apollo 12]] lunar camera sustained damage when it was inadvertently pointed directly towards the Sun damaging its sensor.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Inventor Awaits Data on Moon TV Camera|date=November 19, 1969|work=Star-Gazette}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|title=On Moon TV Camera Failure|date=November 20, 1969|work=Star-Gazette}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|title=Sun-Damaged TV Tube Could Have Been Repaired on Moon|date=December 11, 1969|work=Star-Gazette}}</ref>

In 1969 Westinghouse was awarded the contract for the TV image tube for the [[Viking program]] of 1972. Goetze oversaw the development of the Mars camera.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Westinghouse Awarded Contract for TV Image Tube for Mars Program of 1972|date=November 7, 1969|work=Star-Gazette}}</ref>

The SEC tube was awarded the "Most Meritorious Patent Award" at Westinghouse.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Westinghouse Special Patent Award|last=Goetze|first=Gerhard W|date=August 26, 1969|work=Westinghouse Electric Corporation}}</ref>

=== Lunar Camera Tube Program chronology ===
*September 1963 – First contact with NASA/Houston and Grumman Aircraft to propose use of SEC tube for television transmission from LEM
*May 1964- Formal proposal for a lunar Television Camera made to the Manned Spacecraft Center, Houston, by the Westinghouse Aerospace and Electronic Tube Division
*September 1964 - Camera tube contract let by NASA[[File:NASA Photo AS11-37-5545.jpg|thumb|Lunar camera used to transmit live pictures to Earth and US flag as seen from the Apollo 11 [[Lunar Module Eagle|Lunar Module ''Eagle'']]]]
*September 1964 - First tube start with high-power heater (WX-30293)
*September 1964 - First tube start with low-power heater (WX-31034)
*May 1965 – First flight candidate delivered to Westinghouse Aerospace Division
*July 1966 – First start on the Lunar Camera Tube Program
*May 1969 - [[Apollo 10]] crew send first color television pictures from outer space to Earth<ref>{{Cite news|title=Westinghouse Apollo Camera Brings Praise to Horseheads|date=May 21, 1969|work=Star-Gazette}}</ref>
*July 1969 – Television pictures of man's first steps on the Moon. Through joint efforts, one quarter of the population of the Earth was able to see the first steps of the first men on the Moon. ''[[Life (magazine)|Life]]'' magazine estimated that 600 million people watched the first step on the Moon by Armstrong.<ref name="LIFE special 1969">{{Cite magazine|date=1969|title=To the Moon and Back|magazine=[[Life (magazine)|Life]] |volume=Special Edition}}</ref> "People from 47 countries watched the astronauts&nbsp;... Images of the flag-planting ceremony passed through the fixed-focus lens of the camera, were transformed into electrical impulses, amplified a hundred times and beamed directly to earth."<ref name="LIFE special 1969" />
*The WX-31034 Lunar Camera Tube remains at [[Tranquility Base]] on [[Mare Tranquillitatis]] (Sea of Tranquility) on the Moon's surface.<ref>{{Cite journal|date=Fall 1969|title=Westinghouse Lunar Camera Tube WX-31034 - 20 July, 1969 - Tranquility Base}}</ref>

== Awards and honors ==
*1966 – Goetze's lunar camera tube was named one of the 100 most outstanding scientific and technical achievements by ''Industrial Research Magazine''<ref>''Star-Gazette'', October 9, 1966 –Tube Plant Official Cited for Moon-to-Earth TV Camera</ref>
*1969 – Received his Diamond C International Award from the Soaring Society of America (SSA).<ref>[http://www.ssa.org/BadgesAndRecords?show=blog&id=3105 US Badges] at the Soaring Society of America (select '1969' on pulldown menu); retrieved December 8, 2017</ref>
*1973 – Franklin Institute Award, Longstreth Medal for the conception and development of the secondary electron conduction Tube.<ref name="FranklinInstitute" />
*1984 – Rudolf Diesel Medal Award<ref name="Diesel" />
